cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: A LAN and a WAN differ in geographical area and in ____.
cards.answer: LAN: small area, privately owned, dedicated infrastructure. WAN: large area, public or third-party (leased) infrastructure. Both can be wired or wireless.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: Booking terminals only display the screen. All processing happens on a central server. Thin or thick client?
cards.answer: Thin client [1]: processing and storage happen on the server, so the terminal cannot work without the network [1]. The name alone is only half the marks.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: A full mesh connects 5 devices. How many links does it need?
cards.answer: 10 links: n(n − 1) ÷ 2 = 5 × 4 ÷ 2. A star needs only 5 links plus one switch. That is why a mesh is expensive.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: Star topology. How does a packet get from PC1 to PC3? (3 marks)
cards.answer: PC1 sends the packet to the switch [1]. The switch checks the destination address [1]. It forwards it ONLY to PC3, the intended recipient [1].

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: Two server rooms are 900 m apart, next to a railway with heavy electrical equipment. The best cable is ____.
cards.answer: Fibre-optic carries pulses of light, so it is immune to electromagnetic interference, and the signal barely degrades over 900 m. It costs more, but the reliability justifies it.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: CSMA/CD after a collision. One step is wrong. Tap it.
lines: Listen to the channel (carrier sense)
Send only when the line is idle
A collision is detected
Abort and send a jamming signal
Wait the same fixed time, then resend
cards.answer: Line 5: each device waits a RANDOM time, which grows after repeated collisions. With the same wait they would collide again. Never drop the word 'random'.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: The World Wide Web is ____.
options: a service that runs on the internet
cards.answer: The internet is the physical network of connected networks (the roads). The WWW is the websites on web servers, reached with a browser: one thing driving on the roads.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: You type a URL into a browser. What does the DNS do, and what does it NOT do?
cards.answer: It translates the domain name into the web server's IP address. It does NOT open the page: the web server sends the page and the browser displays it.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: Three of these IPv4 addresses are valid. Tap the invalid one.
cards.answer: 198.168.1.300 is invalid: each IPv4 group is denary 0–255, and 300 > 255. In the exam always give the rule, not just 'invalid'.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: The network 195.12.6.0/23: how many usable host addresses?
cards.answer: 32 − 23 = 9 hostID bits. 2⁹ = 512 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses = 510 usable hosts.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: Going UP the memory hierarchy towards the registers, access time gets shorter and cost per unit ____.
cards.answer: Registers and cache are fastest but cost most per unit, so their capacity is small. That is why a computer needs both primary and secondary storage.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: A CCTV server stores huge video files. Give one reason for magnetic disks instead of SSD, in mark-scheme words.
cards.answer: Lower cost per unit of storage, so the large amount of video is affordable. Or: longer life span under continuous read/write. Never just 'cheaper'.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: How a magnetic hard disk works. One line describes a different device. Tap it.
lines: Several platters spin together at the same speed
Heads on actuator arms move over the surfaces
Data sits in concentric tracks split into sectors
Bits are pits and lands read by a laser
cards.answer: Line 4 is an optical disc. A hard disk stores 1 or 0 as two states of magnetisation: a write current changes the magnetic field, and reading turns the field back into a current.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: A computer sends a document to a slow printer through a buffer. How is the buffer used? (4 marks)
cards.answer: Data goes into the buffer at the computer's speed [1]. The printer takes it at its slower speed [1]. The processor is free for other tasks [1]. When the buffer is empty, an interrupt asks for more [1]. A buffer never 'sends' anything.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: Flash memory must ____ a whole block before it can write to it.
cards.answer: NAND flash: transistor cells, no moving parts. A block is erased 'in a flash', one page is read in one operation. The cells wear out slowly with continuous use.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: Laser printer: what happens first, the toner coats the drum or the laser discharges positions on the drum?
cards.answer: The laser discharges positions first, building an electrostatic image of the page. Then charged toner sticks only where the drum was discharged, and heated rollers fuse it to the paper.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: An architect 3D-prints a model of a building. Explain how it is printed. (3 marks)
cards.answer: Additive manufacturing [1]. A CAD design is split into layers [1]. A nozzle builds the model one layer at a time, repeated for each layer [1]. Finally it is cured.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: A car's lane detection system keeps the car in its lane. Why is it an embedded system? (2 marks)
cards.answer: It is built into the car, a larger system [1]. It performs only one task: keeping the car in its lane [1]. Name the car: 'embedded in another system' alone does not score.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: SRAM against DRAM. One line is wrong. Tap it.
lines: DRAM stores each bit in a capacitor
DRAM must be refreshed every few ms
SRAM stores each bit in a flip-flop
SRAM: lower cost per unit, higher bit density
SRAM is used for cache memory
cards.answer: Line 4 describes DRAM: lower cost per unit and higher bit density, so it is used for main memory. SRAM has the faster access time.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: A router's firmware is updated without taking the chip out. It is stored in ____.
cards.answer: EEPROM is erased by an electrical signal, even one byte at a time, and stays in the circuit. EPROM is erased with ultraviolet light and is usually removed.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: The stored program concept: instructions and ____ are stored in the same memory.
cards.answer: That is the mark: say WHERE. The processor fetches each instruction from main memory and executes them one after another. A new program means a new job.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: The ____ stores the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
cards.answer: Program Counter. The MAR stores the address of the location being read from or written to NOW. Always say what a register stores AND which one.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: The ____ stores data just read from memory or about to be written, and acts as a buffer.
cards.answer: Memory Data Register. It is a buffer because transfers inside the CPU are much faster than outside. The CIR holds the instruction being decoded and executed.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: The ____ bus is one-way: it only carries addresses out of the CPU.
cards.answer: Address bus: one-way, from the MAR. Data bus: two-way, to the MDR. Control bus: two-way, carries timing, read, write and interrupt signals.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: How do the system clock and the control unit work together? (4 marks)
cards.answer: The clock creates timing signals [1], sent on the control bus [1]. On each signal the control unit sends commands to the other components [1], so they are synchronised and steps happen in the right order [1].

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: Why does a higher clock speed improve performance? 'It is faster' scores nothing.
cards.answer: Higher clock speed → more fetch–execute cycles per second → more instructions executed each second. 2 GHz = 2 billion cycles per second.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: A 16-bit address bus. How many memory locations can it address directly?
cards.answer: 2¹⁶ = 65 536. Every extra address bit doubles the number. A 32-bit address bus reaches about 4.3 billion locations.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: The fetch stage in register transfer notation. Tap the wrong line.
lines: MAR ← [PC]
PC ← [PC] − 1
MDR ← [[MAR]]
CIR ← [MDR]
cards.answer: Line 2: the PC is incremented: PC ← [PC] + 1. Also learn line 3: [[MAR]] means the contents of the address held in the MAR.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: The processor checks for interrupts ____.
options: at the end of each fetch–execute cycle
in the middle of the decode stage
cards.answer: Only after the execute stage is complete, before the next fetch. If the interrupt has a higher priority, the registers are saved and the ISR runs.

cards.subject: computer_science
cards.hook: How an interrupt is handled. One line is wrong. Tap it.
lines: A flag is set in the interrupt register
At the end of the F–E cycle, interrupts are checked
Its priority is lower, so the ISR runs now
Registers saved on the stack, ISR address into PC
ISR ends, registers restored, program resumes
cards.answer: Line 3: only an interrupt with HIGHER priority than the current task is handled. A lower one waits, and the fetch–execute cycle simply continues.
